Area.evidence_source: The group of young men who participated in this study understood their desire to die and their subsequent suicide attempt as being a consequence of being disconnected from parents, peers and partners. Their experience of disconnection seemed to be intensified because of their engaging in a range of behaviours, including suppressing their emotions, refusing to seek help, substance use, focusing on work, self-harm behaviours, withdrawing from social interaction and rejecting their religion. The participants believed that disconnecting from others and the self was a viable technique for managing painful emotions and thoughts. However, in hindsight, participants recognised that disconnecting from others and themselves intensified the emotions that they sought to control and thus it became a trigger for suicidal behaviour. They understood suicide as a means of achieving the ultimate disconnection. As observed frequently with men, they chose methods of hanging or initiating a car accident, both considered violent and very lethal methods, to achieve this aim (Denning et al. 2000). Surviving their suicide attempt was interpreted by participants as a 're-birth' and an opportunity to redefine their purpose in life. In the aftermath of their suicide attempt, participants were reminded that others care about them and that close relationships endow life with meaning. Participants said that reconnecting with others helped them to develop a different perspective of themselves and increased their sense of agency and perceived control over their life. Participants said that communicating their emotional distress and seeking help from others were central strategies to protect themselves against becoming suicidal again. All participants in this study reported that relational factors (such as emotional unavailable, strict and controlling parents and being socially marginalised) and their perception of thwarted belongingness initially pushed them towards suicide. However, all participants reported that they gained courage to connect with close others again when close others expressed that participants are loved, respected and form part of their lives. The suicide attempt also created an urgency within participants and close others to communicate with each other more openly and honestly (against the stereotypical masculine expectation of independence and hiding emotions), in order to jointly solve problems and dispel perceptions about not being loved, valued and accepted. Finally, two participants reported that the therapeutic relationship with a psychologist or psychiatrist helped them to evaluate their perceptions and communicate and connect better with others. Paradoxically, participants reported that their suicide attempt allowed them to re-establish connection and find relatedness, which seems to have facilitated their recovery from suicidality. Besides a thwarted sense of belonging, participants also reported that a thwarted sense of autonomy was a contributory cause of their experience of attempting suicide. They explained suicide as a means of asserting their autonomy and they experienced an increased sense of autonomy during their recovery from being suicidal. Not only did they believe themselves to be outsiders in their families and amongst their peers, they also understood themselves to be deficient or less than other men. Their struggle to fit in took place within a cultural context that encouraged conformity to the norm and made it difficult to fit in (Durkheim [1897] 1951). They perceived others (parents, peers and other men) to be unsupportive and rejecting. Over time, participants came to understand themselves as victims and not as agents. Their experience of low agency and interpersonal distance meant that they struggled to develop a healthy autonomous-related self, as described by Kagitcibasi (2005). Participants thought that the solution to their intolerable 'psycheache' (Shneidman 1993) would be to remove themselves from a world that failed to meet their needs for belonging and autonomy. However, the participants' experience of surviving their suicide attempts gave them renewed hope that there might be a way to live meaningfully in spite of not 'fitting in' with the sociocultural ideal, if they formed close relationships with supportive others. In turn, reconnection with close others seems to be an important mechanism for overcoming suicidality, because it allows for the development of an autonomous-related self (Kagitcibasi 2005; Oliffe et al. 2012). Gay participants explained that their experiences across different sociocultural contexts (stigma, stereotyping, religious and cultural expectations and fear of rejection) made them believe that being gay is a defect – something that is shameful and results in rejection by others and God. They said that social constraints with regard to expressing their sexuality resulted in their feeling inferior to others and excluded from social systems, such as their religion. They explained that their wish to kill themselves emerged in response to their strong belief that they did not belong in this world because of being so different. Developing a sexual identity that is not in keeping with the dominant cultural and religious expectations is challenging when sexuality cannot be freely expressed (lack of autonomy) and when authentic and close relationships with others are avoided for fear of rejection and homophobia (lack of relatedness). This resulted in feelings of alienation from others in a context where it was unacceptable to be gay (McAndrew and Warne 2010). Suicide was seen by these participants as the only way to escape this conflict. male suicides were found to be related to failing at a masculine performance of autonomy and authority. The unbearable shame resulting from failing to meet social expectations of being autonomous and authoritative has been found to be a common reason for men to engage in suicidal behaviour across several studies (e.g. Adinkrah 2012). An analysis based on Kagitcibasi's (2005) model of the autonomous-related self suggests that a lack of autonomy seems to be a trigger of female suicidal behaviour, whereas a lack of relatedness appears to be a driver of male suicidal behaviour. This, according to Kagitcibasi (2005), interferes with the healthy development of an autonomous-related self and may predispose men to suicidal behaviour.
